posts.title: When to Throw the Party - A Platform Engineering Problem
posts.description: It's obvious that the DevOps movement destroyed the cultural phenomenon of Release Parties, where Engineering and Product finally came together after a stressful season of crunch, blame and broken promises to get drunk together after the first successful yet random build. At the same time the Ops guys shaved an ever-growing herd of yaks to deploy that particular build in production before daylight (They hadn't been invited anyways). This tradition has been replaced by a rather "boring" assumption that software development is only a success if business value has actually been delivered. Richard Campbell, an industry veteran, coined the phrase "When to throw the party" as a major question. Fast forward almost 20 years, the question is still valid and points towards the coordination effort that makes software engineering so hard to agree on completion. posts.title: Meeting Guidelines are institutional Theater
posts.description: Back in 2007 when I started in IT, receiving a meeting invite was a highlight. Somebody took notice of me and, maybe, even considered me valuable in one way or another. Turns out, most invites we receive in the workplace are actually pretty much the contrary. I) Your boss (or/and his boss) will never read nor care for your organization's meeting guidelines. II) In most cases, that's no big deal. Sooner or later, every organization scaling beyond the magic number of 150 will start a meeting improvement committee coming up with nearly identical meeting guidelines to reduce perceived waste and presumably improve meeting quality. Almost none of them are enforced. None of their effects are measured; it's institutional theater : we receive a signal (meetings are perceived as wasteful) and respond with wishful thinking wrapped in process instead of analyzing cause. posts.title: Fail Fast, Refactor Often - Escaping the Defensive Terraform Trap
posts.description: Scenario Your Terraform apply just failed. Again. For the third time this week, and you're not even sure why. Was it the Azure DevOps provider timing out? That managed identity that existed yesterday but returns 404 today? Or just one of the 247 API calls in your 40-minute deployment hitting a rate limit? Most cloud platforms rely on multiple services running in integration to deliver value. Those are usually configured using Infrastructure as Code like Terraform or Pulumi. By nature, those tools let engineers define desired infrastructure declaratively using providers which abstract the actual API calls required to determine and change the state. As these platforms grow, the configurations become brittle due to the sheer amount of hidden API calls (of which some will fail eventually) and providers that may require updates or show intermittent bugs.
